chapters.title: Work above and below the water
chapters.body: A London Museum helmet record describes a Port of London Authority diver and equipment for speaking with the surface. Divers helped with underwater maintenance and salvage.
chapters.prompt: Look at the helmet windows. How might a diver and a surface team work together when visibility is poor?
chapters.disclosure: The date belongs to the documented museum object, not our 3D model. Our model is an illustration; no ownership or exact reconstruction is claimed.

chapters.title: Ships connect people and places
chapters.body: Empire Windrush reached Tilbury on 22 June 1948 with passengers from the Caribbean and elsewhere. This is one documented example of travel and migration through a port.
chapters.prompt: Compare the working spaces aboard our fishing boat with the different needs of a passenger voyage. What would people need to bring?
chapters.sourceLabel: Royal Museums Greenwich, History of the Windrush
chapters.disclosure: This fishing-boat model is not Windrush and is not claimed to have carried those passengers. No passenger biography is invented here.

chapters.title: Objects cannot tell every story
chapters.body: Royal Museums Greenwich preserves oral histories about maritime life. Personal accounts can help connect shipboard objects to work and everyday experience.
chapters.prompt: Choose a seat, instrument or tool aboard the teaching boat. What question would you ask someone who used it?
chapters.disclosure: No historical recording or quotation is reproduced. Our cabin and log are teaching reconstructions, not evidence of a named person or this boat's history.
